title: DevOps, CI/CD & Observability
summary: CI/CD pipeline design, the three pillars of observability (metrics, logs, traces), monitoring best practices, alerting strategies, and SRE concepts.

explanation.overview: DevOps bridges development and operations — ensuring code is deployed safely, frequently, and automatically. Observability ensures you can understand what's happening inside your production system by examining its external outputs. In system design interviews, you're expected to know how the system is deployed and monitored.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Every commit triggers: code checkout → build → lint → unit tests → integration tests → artifact creation (Docker image, JAR). Fast feedback: developers know within 5-10 minutes if their change broke anything. BEST PRACTICES: (1) Run tests in parallel (split across pods). (2) Cache dependencies (node_modules, Maven .m2). (3) Fail fast (lint first, then unit tests, then slow integration tests). (4) Trunk-based development (short-lived branches, merge to main daily). TOOLS: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, ArgoCD.

Continuous Delivery: after CI passes, the artifact is READY to deploy (manual approval before production). Continuous Deployment: after CI passes, the artifact is AUTOMATICALLY deployed to production (no human approval). Most organizations do Continuous Delivery with automated staging deploy + manual production approval.

Rolling Update (K8s default): replace old pods one at a time with new pods. minAvailable ensures minimum capacity during deploy. Zero downtime but both versions coexist during rollout — APIs must be backward compatible. Blue-Green: two identical environments (Blue = current, Green = new). Deploy to Green, test, then switch traffic (DNS or LB). Instant rollback (switch back to Blue). COST: 2× infrastructure during deploy. Canary: route 1-5% of traffic to new version. Monitor error rate, latency, business metrics. If OK, gradually increase (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%). If problems, rollback immediately. A/B Testing: like canary but based on user segments (new users, specific region, premium tier) for feature evaluation, not just safety.

examples.title: Netflix Spinnaker & Automated Canary Analysis (ACA)
examples.description: How Netflix safely deploys thousands of times a day without human manual testing using statistical canary analysis.
examples.code:
The Problem:
Deploying to 100% of servers at once causes catastrophic global outages if a bug slips through CI. Manual canary deployments (deploying to 1 server and having a human watch the logs) doesn't scale for 1000s of microservices.

The Architecture (Spinnaker + Kayenta):
Netflix open-sourced Spinnaker, their continuous delivery platform. When a developer merges code, Spinnaker starts an 'Automated Canary Deployment'.
1. It spins up three clusters: Production (existing), Baseline (a fresh copy of the old code), and Canary (the new code). *Why Baseline? Because a brand new cold-started pod behaves differently than a pod that has been running for 5 days. Comparing Canary to Baseline ensures an apples-to-apples comparison.
2. It routes 1% of traffic to Baseline and 1% to Canary.
3. Kayenta (the ACA engine) pulls 1,000+ metrics (CPU, memory, HTTP 500s, p99 latency) from both clusters for 30 minutes.
4. It performs statistical T-tests on the metrics. If the Canary deviates negatively from the Baseline by more than a threshold, Spinnaker automatically kills the Canary and aborts the deploy. If it passes, it rolls out to 100%.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Continuous Deployment at scale relies entirely on observability. You cannot do CD without phenomenal, automated metric collection and alerting. Human validation does not scale.

examples.title: Deployment Strategy Matrix
examples.description: Choose the correct deployment rollout strategy in an interview scenario based on risk tolerance and system state.
examples.code:
STRATEGY             | DOWNTIME | ROLLBACK SPEED | COST THOUGH DEPLOY | BEST USED FOR
---------------------|----------|----------------|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------
Recreate             | High     | Very Slow      | Normal             | Stateful legacy systems, Dev environments
Rolling Update       | Zero     | Slow           | Normal             | General microservices (Default K8s behavior)
Blue/Green           | Zero     | Instant        | 2x Normal          | Critical high-traffic services, DB schema changes done carefully
Canary               | Zero     | Fast           | Normal             | Extreme scale (FAANG), risky algorithm changes
A/B Testing          | Zero     | N/A            | Normal             | Product validation (testing if a new button color increases sales)

examples.title: Failure Modes & Exception Handling
examples.description: How to handle catastrophic failures and network partitions in this tier.
examples.code:
try-catch fallback mechanics:
1. NetworkTimeoutException: Trigger circuit breaker and return stale cached data.
2. ConnectionRefusedException: Shift traffic to the standby region (Pilot Light architecture).
3. OOMError: Restart exact instance via Kubernetes Health Probes.

configurable_params.default: Default library settings usually favor CP over AP
configurable_params.effect: You can modify connection timeouts, retry buffers, and max memory limits.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Tuning configuration to drop stale packets reduces latency but requires robust frontend exception handling.

key_concepts.definition: Numeric measurements collected at regular intervals. Types: Counter (monotonically increasing — total requests, total errors), Gauge (point-in-time value — current CPU %, memory usage, active connections), Histogram (distribution of values — request latency split into buckets: <10ms, <50ms, <100ms, <500ms). USE p99 latency, not average (average hides outliers — 99 requests at 10ms + 1 at 10s = average 109ms masks the 10s request). RED Method (rate, errors, duration) for request-driven services. USE Method (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources (CPU, memory, disk). TOOLS: Prometheus (pull-based metric collection, stores time series), Grafana (dashboards), Datadog, CloudWatch. PROMETHEUS INTERNAL: Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints every 15-60 seconds. Data stored as time series: metric_name{label=value} → [(timestamp, value), ...]. PromQL query language: http_requests_total{method='GET', status=~'5..'}. rate() computes per-second rate. histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) computes p99 latency.

Timestamped, unstructured or structured text recording events. STRUCTURED LOGGING: use JSON format — {timestamp, level, service, trace_id, user_id, message, ...}. Enables efficient search and aggregation. NEVER log: passwords, tokens, PII (personal data — GDPR compliance). LEVELS: DEBUG (development only), INFO (normal operations), WARN (unexpected but recovered), ERROR (failure requiring attention). LOG PIPELINE: Application → Fluentd/Filebeat (collect) → Kafka (buffer) → Elasticsearch (store + index) → Kibana (search + visualize). This is the ELK/EFK stack. Elasticsearch inverted index enables full-text search across billions of log lines in milliseconds. LOG RETENTION: 7-30 days hot (Elasticsearch), 90 days warm (cheaper storage), 1 year cold (S3/Glacier for compliance).

Follows a single request across multiple microservices. A trace consists of spans — each span represents one service's processing of the request. Span contains: trace_id (unique per request), span_id, parent_span_id, service name, operation, start time, duration, status, tags. The trace_id is propagated via HTTP headers (traceparent in W3C Trace Context, or X-B3-TraceId in Zipkin format) so every service logs the same trace_id. VISUALIZATION: Jaeger or Zipkin renders a waterfall graph showing how long each service took and the call sequence (Service A → Service B → Service C → Database). USE WHEN: debugging latency (which service is slow?), understanding dependencies (which services are called?), error tracing (which service caused the 500?). TOOLS: Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray, Datadog APM. OpenTelemetry: vendor-neutral standard for metrics, logs, and traces — instrument once, send to any backend.

examples.title: SRE Alerting: PromQL for SLA Violation
examples.description: A real-world Prometheus query to trigger a PagerDuty alert when the 99th percentile latency of the checkout API exceeds 500ms.
examples.code:
# Calculate the 99th percentile latency over the last 5 minutes
# for the '/api/v1/checkout' endpoint.
histogram_quantile(
  0.99, 
  sum by (le) (
    rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{path="/api/v1/checkout"}[5m])
  )
) > 0.500

# How SREs use this:
# This query is placed in an Alertmanager rule. If this expression evaluates 
# to TRUE for more than 2 minutes (to ignore 5-second network blips), 
# Alertmanager fires a webhook to PagerDuty, which calls the on-call engineer's phone.

key_concepts.definition: ALERT ON SYMPTOMS, NOT CAUSES. Bad alert: 'CPU > 90%' (CPU could be high during normal batch processing). Good alert: 'p99 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes' (directly impacts users). Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting: if you're consuming your monthly error budget 10× faster than expected, alert. If 2× faster, warn. PAGES: only page humans for issues requiring immediate action. Use Slack/email for non-urgent. PagerDuty for pages. RUNBOOKS: every alert must link to a runbook — step-by-step instructions to diagnose and resolve the issue. Reduces MTTR.

SLO (Service Level Objective): availability target (99.9% = 8.76 hours downtime/year). Error Budget = 100% - SLO = 0.1% = 43.2 minutes/month of acceptable downtime. IF error budget remaining: deploy fast, take risks. IF error budget exhausted: freeze deployments, focus on reliability. This creates a quantitative framework for balancing feature velocity and reliability. Google SRE: the team that invented this practice.
